content: The review is no longer suitable for updates because liquid-based cytology has replaced traditional smear technology. The significant variability in disease detection rates with cervical smears may be partially attributed to differences in the sampling devices and the techniques used for sample collection. The objective of this analysis was to determine whether the design of the cervical smear collection device influences the rates of inadequate smears and the detection of disease. Additionally, it aimed to evaluate whether the presence of endocervical cells in the smear impacts the detection of disease. The search for relevant studies included the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group trials register and MEDLINE up to July 1997, along with manual searches of 16 journals. The selection criteria included randomized, quasi-randomized, and non-randomized comparative studies that evaluated cervical smear collection devices in women undergoing primary screening, colposcopy after an abnormal smear, or colposcopy following treatment. Data from the studies were independently extracted by two reviewers, and the quality of the studies was assessed. A total of 36 trials and six observational comparative studies were included in the analysis. The Ayre spatula was found to be less effective than extended-tip spatulas for collecting endocervical cells, as demonstrated in eight trials (odds ratio 2.25, 95% confidence interval 2.06 to 2.44). The combination of a spatula with a cytobrush was more effective than using a spatula alone for collecting endocervical cells (odds ratio 3.33, 95% confidence interval 3.05 to 3.63). This combination also improved the rates of obtaining adequate smears (odds ratio 1.51, 95% confidence interval 1.19 to 1.92). Extended-tip spatulas were superior to other designs for detecting dyskaryosis, as shown in seven trials (odds ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.10 to 1.33). Data from two trials and three observational studies indicated that smears containing endocervical cells were more likely to detect dyskaryosis, particularly in cases of severe disease. Furthermore, the proportion of smears with endocervical cells increased with the severity of the disease. The authors concluded that extended-tip spatulas of various designs are more effective than the Ayre spatula for collecting endocervical cells. The most effective combination for sample collection appears to be the use of a cytobrush with an extended-tip spatula. The presence of endocervical cells in smears serves as a reliable and convenient surrogate marker for the ability to detect dyskaryosis and for achieving adequate smear rates. However, further trials are needed to evaluate the ability of the combination of an extended-tip spatula with a cytobrush, compared to the extended-tip spatula alone, in detecting disease.
